evidence.label: A counterexample to the nearby Lagrangian conjecture

headline: Claims a counterexample to Arnold's nearby Lagrangian conjecture, in the cotangent bundle of a product of two spheres.
scope: One closed exact Lagrangian in T*(S⁹ × S^(N−1)) for some sufficiently large even N, which is not given explicitly.
plain: A cotangent bundle is the space of all positions and momenta over a base space. Arnold's nearby Lagrangian conjecture says that a certain kind of closed surface in it, an exact Lagrangian, can always be slid back onto the base. Strong results showed such surfaces always look like the base from the point of view of topology. This paper claims a surface that has the same shape as the base but cannot be slid back. The base is a product of two spheres of very high dimension.
doesNot: This does not give the dimension N explicitly or settle the conjecture for low-dimensional bases such as surfaces. It has no Lean check.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Vladimir Arnold, whose discussion of Lagrangian knots set the problem
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to disprove a central conjecture of symplectic topology that many deep results had supported.

explanation:
Start with a cylinder. Think of its circle as positions q, measured as an angle. Think of its height as a momentum p. This cylinder is the cotangent bundle of the circle, the space of all positions and momenta. The circle at height zero is the zero section. Now draw the closed curve p = cos q. The area between it and the zero section, counted with sign, is the integral of cos q from 0 to 2π, which is 0. A curve with zero signed area like this is called exact. It can be slid back onto the zero section by a Hamiltonian isotopy, a motion that follows the equations of classical mechanics. The curve p = 1 has signed area 2π, so it is not exact. Such a motion keeps signed area, so it cannot bring that curve back.

In higher dimensions the curves become Lagrangians. A Lagrangian is a smooth piece of the same dimension as the base, on which a basic area form vanishes[2]. Exact means a certain one-form on it is the derivative of a function[2]. Arnold's nearby Lagrangian conjecture asks whether every closed exact Lagrangian can be slid back onto the zero section this way[3]. Low-dimensional cases were known, such as the case over the two-sphere[4]. Abouzaid showed that projecting such a Lagrangian to the base is a homotopy equivalence when one class vanishes[5]. Kragh removed that condition[6]. A homotopy equivalence means the two have the same shape up to stretching. Abouzaid and Kragh later proved a finer version. But these results are about topology. They do not say whether the slide exists[7].

The paper claims a no[1]. For some large even N, it builds a closed exact Lagrangian over the product of a 9-sphere and an (N−1)-sphere. The Lagrangian has the same smooth shape as the base, but no slide carries the zero section to it[8]. So the base has dimension 9 + N − 1 = N + 8. N is not given as a number.

The key obstacle is to find a hidden invariant that ordinary topology misses. The paper uses smooth tubes, which are regions shaped like the negative part of a quadratic form. A family of them over the 9-sphere gives a class a. This class a is nonzero, yet its coarser sphere-bundle shadow is trivial[9]. Using Morse theory, the paper shows that a slide to the zero section would make a vanish[10]. The second sphere factor is used to make the Lagrangian embedded, without self-crossings.

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The argument relies on deep results in algebraic K-theory, such as Waldhausen's tube fibration and Rognes's calculations. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark-level claim if it holds: it would disprove Arnold's nearby Lagrangian conjecture in general. The example is in very high dimension, with N not given explicitly. There is no Lean check or published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: The space of all positions on a base space together with all momenta at each position.
The copy of the base inside the cotangent bundle where every momentum is zero.
A smooth piece of the cotangent bundle, of the same dimension as the base, on which the basic area form vanishes.
A Lagrangian on which the canonical one-form is the derivative of a single function.
A smooth motion that follows the equations of classical mechanics for some changing energy function.
A map showing two spaces have the same shape up to continuous stretching.
Studying a space through the critical points, such as peaks and saddles, of a function on it.
A function with extra variables whose critical points describe a Lagrangian.
